rv.q: “Prima Facie” is the kind of theater every artist should have an opportunity to make and every audience an opportunity to experience.
What Comer’s Tessa has to say about her experience must be said, and repeated and repeated, until the world has changed and “Prima Facie” comes to feel like history, and not current events.
Jodie Comer gives one of the most thrilling performances of the Broadway season in "Prima Facie," a gripping solo play by Suzie Miller.
Killing Eve star Jodie Comer claims Broadway as her own in her tour de force performance of Prima Facie, a scalding indictment of the law and its limits opening tonight at the Golden Theatre.
A formidable Broadway attraction, indeed.
It’s an incredible breakneck feat, in which Comer achieves escape velocity from the script of Suzie Miller’s unsteady play and exerts a thrilling and devastating gravitational force of her own.
Comer goes far beyond our basic expectations and into the upper echelons of greatness.
Comer’s performance compensates for the clompy-footed parts of Miller’s script, which falls into a loudly lecturing tone at the end.

I leave it to the jury of theatergoers to determine whether the larger legal argument that Miller makes in Prima Facie follows necessarily from Tessa’s specific experience. But about Comer’s performance there can be no doubt: This is a powerful and moving star turn.

Comer's performance is virtuosic: Martin's direction often helps her achieve moments of tense ecstasy. But the play's important subject matter isn't served, really, by the closed-off nature of the one-person show.
And for that, "Prima Facie" deserves high praise—even adulation.
But the underlining and the advocacy do something odd to the drama: They make it disappear.
The result is a night of theater that not only speaks to the culture but shifts it as well.

With this single role, in which she assumes dozens of hues—sardonic, sexy, comical, enraged, triumphant, joyous, tragic, fiery, rebellious, and so forth—all of it entwined with an extraordinary physical, facial, and vocal expressivity, Ms. Comer leaps into the front ranks of leading British actresses.
Prima Facie is a masterclass in sophistication, thoughtfulness, and brevity; the platonic ideal of a night at the theatre.
Either way, she delivers the most remarkable performance in a season of exceptional acting work.
Comer’s performance and Martin’s staging deepens the text into a one of the most electrifying pieces of theater on Broadway this season.
But it’s Comer’s Tessa, tough and raw, blisteringly believable as she begs to be believed, who wins the case for this play as urgent, necessary theater.
It is both a remarkable and terrifying feat of acting.

The play’s provocative content is sure to provoke strong responses among audience members. But even if one disagrees with its views on the law and justice, there is really no denying that ‘Prima Facie’ makes for gripping theater centered around a thrilling performance and urgent politics.

In her remarkable Broadway debut, Comer gives an emotionally raw and physically demanding performance that drives home the humiliation, betrayal, and feelings of helplessness that accompany sexual assault and its aftermath.
It’s great agit-prop theater, and only time will tell if it has a longer shelf life than Clifford Odets’s play about taxi drivers on strike, first produced in 1935 to great acclaim.
Comer instantly affirms herself as a top-rank theater performer with this dynamic star turn in which she absolutely commands attention for 100 uninterrupted minutes.
It’s a compelling argument, and Comer, under Justin Martin’s vigorous but sensitive direction, makes it soar and sting.
Running 100 unbroken minutes, the production is Exhibit A of how a focused and fierce performance can elevate a work.
Sometimes all an actor needs is an audience and vice versa.

“Prima Facie is an impassioned closing argument disguised as a play. It directly addresses the festering social issue of violence against women in a way that is guaranteed to bring spectators to their feet. And it features a star performance from Jodie Comer that makes it impossible to look away from the stage.
But beneath the surface it’s just fashionable nihilism and emotional blackmail, undergirded by one of the best performances of the season.
After attending a packed matinee, which ended with a standing ovation and the woman seated in front of me simultaneously sobbing and applauding, I’d have to agree it’s worthy of the accolades.
Comer gives a wonderful breathtakingly moving performance, one in which the character changes dramatically and maybe, just maybe, the audience changes as well.
But this play still works because it’s told through one person’s increasingly sensitized perspective.

cn.t: Critics hail Jodie Comer's tour de force Broadway debut as a lawyer-turned-assault-survivor, though some find Suzie Miller's one-woman play too didactic. Comer's physically and emotionally exhausting performance elevates material that occasionally prioritizes polemic over nuance.

vs.sum: The John Golden Theatre offers good sightlines from most seats, though sound quality can vary, especially under the mezzanine. Seating comfort is typical of older theaters with tight legroom, but the venue maintains a pleasant ambiance overall. Facilities are adequate, though not exceptional.

acc.note: 5 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. No wheelchair-accessible restroom (use adjacent Schoenfeld).
